* This is part two in a series that explores drivers of CPS’ FY27 deficit, currently projected at $732M.

→ Bottom line: Revenue is up 34% since FY19. Personnel costs are up 55%. Personnel growth absorbed 92 cents of every new revenue dollar CPS brought in, leaving just 8 cents for everything else in the operating budget.

For example, in FY26, CPS' required contribution to the Chicago Teachers Pension Fund outpaced revenue from the dedicated pension levy, forcing the district to divert $61.3M to cover the shortfall. As required payments continue to rise, these diversions will likely increase.

For context, inflation over the same period grew 28% or roughly 3.7% per year (Bureau of Labor Statistics).

Increased compensation also includes higher pension costs to the district.

Meeting those needs explains some of this increase, a topic I’ll cover in a later post.

Better compensation (~$1.0B in increased cost)
The average CPS salary for all employees grew from $64,000 to $81,000 between FY19 and FY26 (27%), or roughly 3.5% per year.

Note that declining enrollment doesn’t mean a decrease in need. Learning gaps that emerged during the pandemic required intensive support for many students. 

At the same time, the number of students with Individual Education Programs (IEPs) grew from 51,000 to 55,000 (8%).

From FY19 to FY26, total staff grew by about 8,700 (24%), from 36,855 to 45,550

■ School-based positions: + ~6,000 (19%), from 31,370 to 37,399 
■ Citywide roles: + ~2,100 (48%), from 4,344 to 6,432 
■ Central office and network roles: + ~600 (51%), from 1,141 to 1,719

CPS personnel costs rose from $3.96B in FY19 to $6.15B in FY26, a 55% increase. Revenue rose only 34% over the same period, from $7.01B to $9.39B

Two major drivers:
1️⃣ More staff (~$1.2B in increased cost)
2️⃣ Better compensation (~$1.0B in increased cost)

Personnel costs account for $6.15B (71%) of CPS' $8.7B operating budget, the largest piece of total spending. That's reasonable: it takes a lot of people to teach, feed, transport, and support students

❓Why this matters:
CPS faces a projected $500M+ operating deficit in FY27.
$41M isn’t a solution—but it’s ~8% of the gap, equivalent to ~360 teaching positions. Decisions like this signal how CPS plans to address much larger fiscal challenges ahead.

If pursued, the $41M roughly breaks down as:
• $24M for CPS’s general education levy
• $11M for the teachers’ pension levy
• $6M for sped transportation

❓The Board’s choices:
1️⃣ Leave the levy as-is
2️⃣ Approve some/all of the $41M
(FY26 levy must be finalized by 12/29)

❓Why is $41M “available” now?
Earlier this year, CPS set its property tax levy below the maximum allowed under state law.
Because final property values came in higher than expected, CPS now has the legal option—though not the obligation—to levy up to $41M more.

Today, the Chicago Board of Education is holding a special meeting to consider whether to pursue up to $41M in additional property tax revenue.

For over 60% of CPS principals, this will be their first time managing through such a deficit, and they’re doing so amid major leadership transitions at the district level. This week, I spent time with more than two dozen principals and program partners. Here’s what I heard:
Chicago’s school leaders are facing real challenges — and showing real resolve. As I’ve shared, Chicago Public Schools (CPS) is confronting its first significant budget deficit since 2017.

🛠️ So what could help?

✅ Declare more surpluses
✅ Shrink some TIFs
✅ End others entirely

Each step would mean more funding (and would require real discussion!).

💸 What’s a TIF surplus?

If a TIF has money left over, the city must return it to public agencies, including CPS.

Since CPS receives approximately 50% of property taxes, it also receives approximately 50% of the surplus.

In FY25, CPS received $298M, up from $159M in FY24.

TIFs are complicated and a powerful tool.

If we’re serious about fully funding our public schools, we must talk more about them.

🏫 But here’s the catch:

While a TIF is active, CPS and other agencies do not receive the new tax revenue.

In 2025 alone, $1.2B went into TIF funds. 

CPS says it’s missing out on ~$600M/year that could support students and staff.

🙋‍♀️ What’s a TIF?

It’s a tool cities use to boost development in specific neighborhoods.

The city “freezes” how much tax money schools & others get, and uses the anticipated and new tax revenue to fund projects like roads & parks in that same area.

💰 Chicago has been using TIFs since 1983.

There are ~136 TIF districts.

They last 23 years, but the city can request that the state extend them for an additional 12 years.

In Dec 2024, 8 TIFs got extended. Another 10 could follow by 2027.

Chicago Public Schools is facing a projected $539M budget gap in 2026.

There’s no single fix—but we do need to talk about Tax Increment Financing (TIF). 🧵

Closing the gap = raising revenue, cutting costs, or both.

Options are limited.

The City of Chicago could increase TIF funding again (as they did in FY25).
Stay tuned for more potential solutions later this week.
